x.A: Instances in a second AZ with Route 53 routing helps, but DNS-based routing doesn't remove unhealthy instances as quickly or evenly as a load balancer.
x.B: An NLB works at the transport layer (layer 4) and distributes traffic across instances in multiple AZs, which gives high availability for TCP or UDP applications at low cost.
x.C: Adding an ALB as well isn't needed, because the application uses the transport layer, and two load balancers cost more.
x.D: An Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs with application health checks replaces failed instances and keeps capacity in more than one AZ.
x.E: A CloudWatch alarm to restart stopped instances only helps for one type of failure in one AZ, and doesn't give multi-AZ availability.

x.A: Running the form in ECS keeps containers running all month, which costs more than needed for fewer than 100 visits, and SES to a third-party provider adds work.
x.B: API Gateway and Lambda serve the form and handle submissions, and SNS emails the company. You pay per request, so it costs almost nothing for fewer than 100 visits.
x.C: Amplify Hosting with server-side scripting costs more than S3 with serverless functions, and SQS can't send email to the company.
x.D: EC2 instances running Windows Server with IIS costs more and needs management, and WorkMail is a paid mailbox service.

x.A: A single shared email address for all accounts is a single point of failure and weakens security, since many people would have access to the root user email.
x.B: Using a different distribution list for each business unit's root email, with administrators who can respond, and alternate contacts for billing, security, and operations teams routes each notification category to the right people without relying on one person's mailbox.
x.C: Using one person's individual mailbox for root email ties critical notifications to that person, so they'd be missed if the person leaves or is unavailable.
x.D: Aliases to a centralized mailbox concentrate access for all root users in one place, and a single list for each category across all business units doesn't route notifications by business unit.

x.A: Retrying purchases with new instances adds load and doesn't remove the cause of timeouts, and RDS Proxy alone doesn't buffer bursts.
x.B: ElastiCache in front of Aurora reduces the load of repeated reads, so the database handles peak demand better.
x.C: An SQS queue absorbs purchase request bursts, and an Auto Scaling group of workers reads from it at a sustainable rate, so purchases aren't dropped or timed out.
x.D: A Lambda function that retries purchases adds load on the database and doesn't buffer requests.
x.E: An API Gateway usage plan throttles requests, which would reject customers during peak usage.

x.A: DataSync copies data between storage systems, and QuickSight doesn't use DataSync to query a report.
x.B: QuickSight can use Athena to query the Cost and Usage Report data in S3 and show NAT gateway costs by day in a dashboard that can be shared with senior leadership.
x.C: CloudWatch dashboards show metrics, not detailed cost report data, and DataSync isn't a query service.
x.D: CloudWatch dashboards don't query the Cost and Usage Report through Athena to produce a table visual of daily costs.

x.A: Setting the CloudFront default TTL to 2 minutes caches objects at the edge for 2 minutes, so stale content is served for no more than a few minutes.
x.B: S3 has no default TTL setting for CloudFront caching. Caching is controlled by CloudFront settings and object headers.
x.C: A Cache-Control private directive stops shared caches like CloudFront from caching the objects, so it doesn't improve performance with caching.
x.D: A Lambda@Edge function to add Expires headers on viewer response adds cost and complexity, and the Expires header only affects browsers.
x.E: A long max-age of 24 hours caches for better performance, and creating a CloudFront invalidation on deployment clears changed files from the edge caches immediately, so stale content isn't served.

x.A: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers only EC2, so the growing Lambda usage wouldn't be discounted.
x.B: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan doesn't cover Lambda, and a public subnet isn't how Lambda reaches the private instances.
x.C: A Compute Savings Plan covers both EC2 and Lambda usage, and connecting the functions to the private subnets lets them reach the EC2 instances directly.
x.D: A function in the Lambda service VPC can't directly reach EC2 instances in private subnets.

x.A: Tagging, Config rules, and Lambda termination add a lot to build, and terminating resources doesn't limit costs by budget. Cost Explorer reports only show spending.
x.B: AWS Budgets for each developer account sends alerts on actual and forecast spend, and Budgets actions apply a DenyAll policy to the developer's role once the budget is reached, so costs stop. It's built in and needs little work.
x.C: Cost Explorer and Cost Anomaly Detection only report and alert and don't limit spending.
x.D: Service Catalog and Lambda functions to stop resources every day need custom work and don't enforce a spending limit.

x.A: The web tier's security group allows HTTPS only from the ALB's security group, so only the load balancer can reach the web servers.
x.B: Allowing outbound HTTPS to anywhere isn't needed. Security groups are stateful, and the web tier doesn't need internet access.
x.C: The database tier allows SQL Server traffic only from the application tier's security group, which keeps it closed to everything else.
x.D: Security groups are stateful, so outbound rules aren't needed to reply, and the database doesn't initiate traffic to the web tier.
x.E: The application tier allows inbound HTTPS only from the web tier's security group, so only the web servers can call the business logic.
x.F: The application tier doesn't need outbound rules to the web tier, because responses are allowed automatically, and SQL Server traffic goes to the database tier, not the web tier.

x.A: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan doesn't cover SageMaker, since SageMaker has its own plan.
x.B: A Compute Savings Plan doesn't cover SageMaker. SageMaker needs its own Savings Plan.
x.C: A SageMaker Savings Plan covers SageMaker usage, which no other plan includes.
x.D: A Compute Savings Plan covers Lambda, Fargate, and EC2, so one plan discounts three of the four services.
x.E: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers only EC2, not Fargate, and is less flexible.

x.A: SCT can convert schema and some application SQL, but rewriting all the SQL in the applications is a lot of code change, which the company wants to minimize.
x.B: Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL understands the SQL Server T-SQL dialect and wire protocol, so applications can run their SQL Server queries with minimal code changes.
x.C: SCT converts the database schema, and DMS migrates the data, which covers the database migration.
x.D: RDS Proxy pools connections and doesn't translate SQL Server queries to PostgreSQL.
x.E: DMS migrates data and doesn't rewrite application SQL queries.

x.A: Setting the EC2 account attribute to always encrypt new EBS volumes makes every new volume encrypted by default in the Region, and unencrypted volumes can't be created.
x.B: A Config rule detects unencrypted volumes after they exist, and doesn't prevent their creation or turn on default encryption.
x.C: Systems Manager creating encrypted copies is a manual fix after the fact, and doesn't prevent unencrypted volumes.
x.D: Migration Hub doesn't use a key to enforce encryption of EBS volumes.

x.A: Kinesis Data Streams in on-demand mode scales automatically with fluctuating traffic, and Lambda processes the clickstream data in real time. Both are serverless.
x.B: Firehose delivers to destinations with buffering, and Glue streaming isn't for real-time analysis in this way.
x.C: Kinesis Video Streams is for video, not clickstream data.
x.D: Managed Service for Apache Flink processes streams and doesn't capture data. It reads from a stream.

x.A: CloudTrail records API calls, so it can't list all buckets that are not versioning-enabled across Regions.
x.B: S3 Storage Lens gives organization-wide visibility into buckets across Regions and accounts, including which buckets don't have versioning enabled.
x.C: IAM Access Analyzer for S3 finds buckets with public or cross-account access, not their versioning status.
x.D: A Multi-Region Access Point routes requests across buckets, and doesn't report on bucket versioning.

x.A: Glacier Instant Retrieval keeps the files immediately accessible across multiple AZs, and it has the lowest storage cost of the instant-access classes for rarely accessed data. Deleting after 4 years completes the lifecycle.
x.B: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so files that can't be recreated could be lost.
x.C: Standard-IA costs more per GB than Glacier Instant Retrieval for data rarely accessed after 30 days.
x.D: Moving files to Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 4 years is pointless since they're deleted then, and Standard-IA costs more than Instant Retrieval.

x.A: Using regional endpoints means the application has to pick the closest one and handle failover itself, and traffic crosses the public internet.
x.B: An active-passive configuration doesn't send data to the nearest bucket, since one Region is passive.
x.C: Regional endpoints require the application to choose a bucket and fail over, and replication across accounts isn't needed.
x.D: A Multi-Region Access Point with a single global endpoint in an active-active configuration routes requests to the nearest bucket over the AWS global network, avoids public internet congestion, and fails over automatically. Cross-Region Replication keeps the buckets in sync.

x.A: An Auto Scaling group with a minimum and maximum of one replaces the instance automatically if it fails, so the application recovers without design changes. Using the AMI and an ALB makes it reliable and fault tolerant.
x.B: Backups with a manual DR process means downtime while restoring, so it isn't fault tolerant.
x.C: Launching two copies of a legacy application can break it, because it may not support running more than one instance, and the designs can't be changed.
x.D: Refactoring the applications into containers needs design changes, which aren't allowed.

x.A: Control Tower creates accounts with automatic guardrails, and a networking account with shared subnets through RAM centrally manages the networking, so workload accounts launch resources in the shared subnets. It needs the least work.
x.B: Organizations alone doesn't apply automatic guardrails to new accounts like Control Tower does.
x.C: A VPC in each account with an inspection VPC and transit gateways means managing networking in every account, which isn't central management.
x.D: Organizations doesn't add guardrails, and per-account VPCs with transit gateway attachments is more to manage.

x.A: S3 hosts the static content cheaply, and CloudFront caches it at the edge, which reduces cost as traffic grows, with no servers to run.
x.B: ElastiCache can't be configured to serve an S3 bucket's website content.
x.C: An ALB can't point to an Amplify website, and it adds cost.
x.D: EC2 instances for caching add cost and management.

x.A: A Volume Gateway presents iSCSI block volumes, not SMB file shares, and it runs as a gateway to manage.
x.B: A Tape Gateway is for backup software and virtual tapes, not SMB file shares.
x.C: A Windows file share on EC2 means managing the instance, so it has more administrative overhead.
x.D: FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed service that supports SMB, so it needs the least administration.

x.A: A cross-Region Aurora read replica could work, but promoting it manually adds time and steps, and an Aurora global database is the purpose-built option.
x.B: An Aurora global database replicates storage to another Region with typically under a second of lag, which meets an RPO of 5 minutes, and managed failover meets the RTO of 20 minutes with minimal configuration changes.
x.C: A separate cluster with cross-Region replication takes more configuration to set up and manage than a global database.
x.D: DMS to sync the clusters needs a replication instance and tasks to manage, and it adds lag.

x.A: A Fargate task can run for as long as needed without interruptions, and EventBridge Scheduler runs it weekly. It's a managed, stateful-friendly option for a job of at least an hour.
x.B: Lambda has a 15 minute limit, so a job that needs at least an hour can't run there.
x.C: Spot Instances can be interrupted, and the job is stateful and can't tolerate interruptions.
x.D: DataSync copies data and doesn't run analysis jobs.

x.A: A Lake Formation data lake with Glue crawlers needs a lot of setup, and security data from different services needs normalization.
x.B: A Lambda function collecting data in .csv format is custom development to build and maintain.
x.C: Security Lake automatically centralizes security data from AWS sources and partners into a data lake in your account (in S3) in a standard format, so it takes the least development effort.
x.D: DMS replicates databases and isn't a way to collect security data.

x.A: Software VPN tunnels between VPCs need to be managed and don't scale easily to 100 applications.
x.B: VPC peering needs a connection and routes for each pair of VPCs, and it isn't transitive, so connecting all applications to each other doesn't scale to over 100 VPCs.
x.C: Direct Connect connects on-premises networks to AWS and isn't used to connect VPCs to each other.
x.D: A transit gateway is a central hub. Each application VPC and the shared services VPC attach to it, and routes allow all of them to communicate, so adding more than 100 applications only means adding attachments.

x.A: ECS with the Fargate launch type runs the cloud containers, and ECS Anywhere (external launch type) runs the same containers on the on-premises servers, so one ECS cluster covers both.
x.B: An ALB handles HTTP traffic for the ECS services running in the cloud.
x.C: An NLB works at layer 4 and isn't needed for HTTP traffic, because an ALB provides HTTP features.
x.D: Fargate can't run on premises. On-premises containers use ECS Anywhere.
x.E: ECS Anywhere uses the external launch type, not Fargate.
